desc:
Given points, an array of integer points [x, y], find the largest Manhattan distance between two of them. The Manhattan distance is |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|. Comparing every pair is too slow for large inputs.

points = [[1,1],[3,5],[-2,4]]
(1,1)-(3,5) = 6,  (1,1)-(-2,4) = 6,  (3,5)-(-2,4) = 6
result = 6
hints: Rotate the plane by 45 degrees: look at x + y and x - y for each point.
The Manhattan distance equals the larger of the two differences |(x1 + y1) - (x2 + y2)| and |(x1 - y1) - (x2 - y2)|.
The maximum over all pairs of the larger of two quantities is the larger of the two maxima over pairs, and each of those is a spread of values: max minus min.
editorial: For any two points, |dx| + |dy| = max(|d(x + y)|, |d(x - y)|), a standard identity. Since the maximum over all pairs of a maximum of two terms is the maximum of the two separate maxima, the answer is max(maxS - minS, maxD - minD), where S holds the values x + y and D holds x - y.
The largest difference inside a list is its maximum minus its minimum, so one pass over the points gives the answer. The work is O(n) and needs no pair comparisons.
The result is at most 2 * 10<sup>9</sup>, which fits in a 32-bit signed integer, so the constraint on coordinates keeps the answer in range.
